content: In the previous section, it was reported that nearly half of the surveyed facilities lacked a clear definition of adherence. However, only 4% of facilities reported having no clear definition of loss to follow-up (LTFU). The most common definition of LTFU used by facilities was when an adolescent had not attended a clinic visit for three or more months (66%). The second most common definition was missing two or more consecutive visits (15%). Box 5 highlights the specificity of LTFU definitions in the sample and cautions against assumptions when interpreting the rate of guidelines and protocols in place at facilities. Forty-one percent of respondents indicated that no guidelines or protocols were in place for managing adolescents facing retention challenges. Where such guidelines existed, the most common interventions included home visits (52%) and telephone calls (44%). Less than two-thirds (61%) of facilities offered services to support adolescent retention in care, which is slightly lower than the 67% adherence support rate reported in the previous section. Regional differences were noted, with East African facilities being the most likely to offer retention services (82%), followed by Southern Africa (64%) and West and Central Africa (31%). Feedback from respondents regarding retention definitions and guidelines revealed that LTFU is often defined as the inability to contact a client via phone or locate them in their community, combined with their failure to attend clinic appointments for six months (if not on ART) or three months (if on ART). Some facilities relied on phone calls to remind clients of appointments rather than formal guidelines. When adolescents were identified as LTFU, 76% of facilities conducted home visits, 50% made telephone calls, and 30% involved community health workers or community-based organizations (CBOs) in follow-up efforts. Less commonly, facilities used SMS, email, or school visits (<5%). Peer support, activities, and clubs (34%) and home visits (31%) were the most common approaches to improving retention. Other approaches, such as general counseling, caregiver engagement, and treatment support, were reported by fewer than 20% of facilities. Respondents frequently cited peer support and home visits as the most effective retention strategies, though these views were largely anecdotal and lacked targeted research. Regarding service delivery, 35% of facilities reported attending to adolescent patients separately from adults and children. In contrast, 31% of facilities attended to all age groups together, 21% grouped adolescents with children, and 8% grouped them with adults. East African facilities were more likely to adopt adolescent-specific service models (56%) compared to Southern Africa (35%) and West and Central Africa (7%). Where separate services were offered, the most common feature was a dedicated clinic day or time for adolescents (88%), followed by dedicated clinic staff (10%) and dedicated clinic space (8%). The age at which adolescents transitioned out of pediatric services varied widely, with the most common age being 18 years (23%), followed by 10 years (14%), 12 years (12%), 15 years (12%), and 20 or 21 years (7% each). Just over half (51%) of facilities had guidelines or protocols to guide the transition process. Transition-specific counseling was provided by 63% of facilities, typically over three sessions lasting more than 15 minutes each. Counseling focused primarily on the transition process itself, with less emphasis on sexual and reproductive health (SRH), adherence, HIV disease management, emotional well-being, and other psychosocial topics. Pregnant adolescents were often transitioned into adult services earlier than standard procedures, with limited support provided during this process. SRH services were offered to HIV-infected adolescents at 63% of facilities, with East African facilities being the most likely to provide these services (84%), followed by Southern Africa (68%) and West and Central Africa (27%). The most common SRH services included family planning and contraceptives (72%), general counseling and health education (40%), and STI screening and treatment (31%). Cervical cancer screening, PMTCT, antenatal care, and voluntary medical male circumcision were offered less frequently (10-14%). The study highlights significant gaps in the availability of adolescent-specific HIV treatment and care services in sub-Saharan Africa. Many facilities lack standardized definitions of adolescence, age-disaggregated data collection, and guidelines for managing adherence, retention, and transitioning. Peer support and home visits were identified as effective strategies for improving adherence and retention, but these approaches were not universally implemented. The findings underscore the need for standardized guidelines, improved data collection, and expanded adolescent-friendly services to address the unique needs of this population. Additionally, further research is needed to evaluate the effectiveness of peer-based interventions and to address systemic barriers to care.
